explanation: The text says these murals help communities by enhancing public spaces and addressing local issues, which are positive contributions, so the art initiatives "enrich" their communities. "Avoid," "predict," and "deny" don't describe benefiting a community in multiple ways.

The dark blue water contrasts with the light blue of the nearby shallows, so the holes are easy to tell apart, or be "differentiated from," those areas. That contrast is why boaters spot them. "Explored by" doesn't fit, since the shallow areas don't explore anything, and "surpassed by" and "elevated from" make no sense here.

Because outside conditions can change the temperature in the cargo area, drivers need equipment that monitors and adjusts the refrigeration. The conditions therefore make that equipment necessary, or "necessitate" its use. "Obviating" means the opposite (making it unnecessary), and "extolling" (praising) and "rescinding" (canceling) don't fit.

Higher prices plus loyal customers would greatly improve, or "transform," the financial outlook for small farms. "Overshadow" and "interpret" don't describe this positive effect, and "hasten" (speed up) doesn't make sense with "financial outlook."

The text says the automobile's influence "extended far beyond" how people traveled and lists effects on communities, city layouts, and personal freedom, so its purpose is to discuss the car's widespread impact. Changes to city roads are only one detail, so B is too narrow, and the text never mentions negative effects (C) or how early cars worked (D).

The text first describes the Museo de Las Americas (founded 1991) and then turns to a "more recently founded" institution, the National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts and Culture. That matches B. The text says nothing about expansion plans (A), doesn't argue for any influence on society (C), and no institution rejects a trend (D).

The sentence before the underlined one says a small sample size can lead to biased analysis, and the underlined sentence adds that such analysis can produce reports of exaggerated effects. So it explains a further possible consequence of Pimentel's small sample. It doesn't counter Clark's objection (D); it extends it. It also doesn't stress how large the reported effect was (C).

fix.passage: In 2016 Marta S. Pimentel and colleagues published a study concluding that ocean acidification has a strong effect on the behavior of Sparus aurata, a species of fish. However, Pimentel and colleagues’ study relied on a mean sample size of only 12 fish. In a 2022 review of various scientists’ conclusions about the impacts of ocean acidification on fish behavior, Timothy D. Clark and colleagues caution that relying on such a relatively small sample size can increase the potential for biased analysis. <u>Such analysis, in turn, can contribute to reports of exaggerated effects.</u>

explanation: The last sentence says the database helps researchers and "informs city planning and conservation efforts." Nothing in the text mentions tourists, extinction, or ranking green spaces by popularity.

It isn't mainly real data (A). Nothing says it weights common scenarios (B) or focuses mainly on unusual ones (C).

The claim is that the speaker wants to make art with universal appeal across generations. Choice B says she wants to make "songs for the people, / Songs for the old and young," which covers both all people and all ages. Choice A says the world needs music but doesn't mention appealing to different generations.

The claim is that Newland comes late because he enjoys anticipating a pleasure. Choice A says thinking about a coming pleasure often satisfied him more than the pleasure itself, which explains the delay. Choice B says he arrived late but gives no reason related to anticipation.

Even though she was a very private person, she personally answered thousands of fan letters about the Moomins, which shows that commitment. Choice A, quitting the comic strip, points the other way, and D only says she did other work too.

After "with," the phrase needs a noun followed by an -ing form: "with Hirao rhythmically shaping trees to music." This phrase describes how the performance unfolds. Finite verbs like "shapes" or "shaped" can't follow "with Hirao" in this structure, and "shape" doesn't work either.

It opens with a comma after "that," so it must close with a matching comma. A dash or semicolon can't pair with the opening comma, and leaving out punctuation leaves the phrase unclosed.

Choices C and D leave two independent clauses ("Tessler extracted..." and "she forged...") joined by only a comma, which is a comma splice. explanation: The text describes events in time order: first citizens vote, then the winners take office. "Afterward" shows that sequence. Nothing is being contrasted or used as an example, so "However," "Instead," and "For example" don't fit.

The cooler air sinks while the warm air rises, and together these make the circular current. "As this occurs" shows the two things happen at the same time. The sentence isn't a summary, an alternative, or an example.

"That said" brings in this qualification, and the claim that it may not remove all the pollutant matches the detail that follows. Choices B and C keep praising the plant and don't lead into the limitation.

Mrs. Hilbery talks sadly about how the great days of the nineteenth century have passed, so "lament" means to regret or mourn. She isn't predicting ("expect"), rejecting ("repudiate"), or listing ("enumerate") those days.

The text explains Beal's 1879 seed-burial experiment and says researchers still dig up bottles, most recently in 2021. That makes it an ongoing experiment. There is only one experiment, so A is wrong, and the text doesn't focus on preservation problems (B) or getting rid of plants (D).

Both texts describe needlework that began as practical mending (sashiko strengthens fabric; kantha joins layers and covers holes) but is also valued for its beauty, as with striking motifs and designer garments. So both suggest the look of these techniques reflects their practical roots and goes beyond them. Choice D fits only Text 1, which emphasizes patterns. One theory says limits on officeholders' enrichment cause growth, and the other says growth causes such bureaucracies. Ang says both wrongly assume one-way causation, since neither factor is independent of the other. So she would say these initiatives can't be explained simply as a cause or simply as a result of growth. Choice A repeats modernization theory's one-way view.

In all three trials, hornworms ate a smaller share of emitting leaves than of nonemitting leaves (for example, about 1.5% vs. 4.6% in Trial 1), but they still ate some emitting leaves. So the compound reduces consumption without fully preventing it. The graph doesn't show how many individual hornworms were deterred (A) or whether the compound is toxic (D).

fix.passage: Some plants’ leaves emit a chemical compound (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) that is thought to be a defense against insects. Researchers modified leaves of the same plant species so that some emitted the compound and others didn’t, then placed hornworms—leaf-eating insects—between leaves of both types and allowed the hornworms to feed for 90 minutes.

Both Y. evonymella and A. caja are noxious, and their ranges overlap. Their warning sounds are nearly identical, so the logical conclusion is mutual protective mimicry between two chemically defended species. Choice B describes harmless species copying harmful ones, but Y. evonymella is itself noxious. Choices C and D generalize beyond the single species studied.

The apparent spread may therefore partly reflect a richer sample, so earlier conclusions may have overstated the broader demographic shift. explanation: "Revolutionizing the field of economic research" describes the 2003 publication and finishes the first sentence. "Before its release" begins a new independent clause, so a period is needed after "research." Choices A and D link two independent clauses with only a comma or nothing, and B leaves a fragment.

A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses. A comma would create a comma splice, and no punctuation would create a run-on.

A finite verb like "indicates," "can indicate," or "will indicate" would create a second independent clause joined by only a comma (a comma splice).

The main clause "The process ... depends on specialized geological conditions" is complete. The rest, "the gems typically forming as hydrothermal fluids interact...," is an absolute phrase, which needs the -ing form. Finite verbs such as "form" or "will form" would create a comma splice.

explanation: To tell the theories apart, the sentence must say how they differ in answering the truth-maker objection. A does this: Lucretianism uses past-tensed properties, while ersatz presentism uses an abstract time outside time. B wrongly says Bourne accepted past-tensed properties, C wrongly says one theory thinks nothing makes past truths true, and D wrongly says Bourne rejected presentism.

fix.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Philosophers espousing presentism (the view that only present things exist) must contend with the truth-maker objection (TO).
• TO: If past things don’t exist, what makes true statements about the past (e.g., “dinosaurs existed”) true? 1996: Presentist philosopher John Bigelow proposed “Lucretianism.”
• Lucretianism posits that the statement is made true by the world’s acceptance of the past-tensed property of “having contained dinosaurs.”
• 2006: Presentist philosopher Craig Bourne proposed “ersatz presentism.” Ersatz presentism posits that the statement is made true by an abstract (“ersatz”) time that exists outside temporal time and represents how things were in the past.

fix.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Prehistoric rock art in the Kimberley region of Australia consists of several distinct styles across various time periods.
• Irregular Infill Animal Period (IIAP) rock art from 13,000 to 17,000 years ago consists of naturalistic animal figures showing detailed features and a variety of poses.
• Gwion rock art from 12,000 to 14,000 years ago features elaborately ornamented anthropomorphic figures.
• Wanjina rock art from up to 5,000 years ago features human ancestor figures along with animal motifs.
• A 2025 study of Kimberley rock art by Ana Paula Motta et al. identified 98 figures depicting outlines of animal forms with simple anatomical details and posed predominantly in profile.
• The study’s superimposition analysis showed that these Linear Naturalistic Figures (LNF) consistently appear on top of Gwion and underneath Wanjina figures.

note: B ("categorical departure from the previous period") is a plausible distractor; D chosen because it is directly grounded in the study's superimposition finding.
